## Bug Description

When Telegram DM topic mode is enabled (`telegram_dm_topic_mode.enabled=1` for a chat), the root DM becomes a lobby: `_run_agent`'s pre-dispatch gate (`_is_telegram_topic_root_lobby` in `gateway/run.py`) returns early for any dm-keyed event whose `thread_id` is empty or "1" (General). For a human typing in the root chat this is intended behavior (they may get a lobby reminder).

But the same gate also swallows **internal kanban notifier wake events** (`MessageEvent(internal=True)` synthesized in `gateway/kanban_watchers.py`): a completion wake keyed `dm` with no `thread_id` returns `None` with **nothing logged at INFO** — the completion notification text still delivers to the chat, but the orchestrator agent never runs, so the workflow silently stalls (no synthesis, no downstream routing, no error anywhere).

## Who hits this

- Any task created **before** topic mode was enabled for the chat (its `kanban_notify_subs` row has no `thread_id`) that completes **after** — its wake vanishes.
- Any subscription created without a thread (dashboard, scripts, or the #56580 wake path once chat_type is fixed to dm — cross-ref: measured details in https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/56580#issuecomment-4961303842).

Task completions created *from a topic lane* are fine — `HERMES_SESSION_THREAD_ID` flows into the subscription and the wake routes to the topic session.

## Repro (v0.18.2)

1. Telegram DM with topic mode enabled for the chat.
2. Insert a `kanban_notify_subs` row for a task with `thread_id=''` and a dm-shaped source (`chat_id == user_id`), task with non-empty `session_id`.
3. Complete the task.
4. Observed: `kanban notifier: woke agent for <task>` logs, notification text delivers, then nothing — no `inbound message`, no conversation turn, no warning.

## Expected

One of:
- Internal wake events bypass the lobby gate (they are not a human typing in the wrong place), OR
- The wake re-routes to the creator session / last-active topic lane, OR
- At minimum, a WARNING log: swallowing an internal event should never be silent.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.18.2 (Docker, `ghcr.io/nousresearch/hermes-agent`), Telegram gateway, single-profile orchestrator + kanban dispatcher embedded in gateway.

items.title: RFC: Adversarial review and automation approval matrix for Discord Spec Factory
items.body:
## Summary

The Discord Spec Factory currently has the right high-level safety posture—repository-local Spec Kit state is canonical, role/profile/model routing is explicit, and local-git/remote-GitHub effects require approval—but the process needs a deliberate adversarial review before more automation is enabled.

Please review the end-to-end factory as an approval-matrix problem: identify which stages can be automated, which require human approval, what evidence must be persisted, and which controls must fail closed under hostile or ambiguous input.

## Scope to adversarially review

Review each boundary in the flow:

1. **Discord intake and source packet creation**
   - spoofed/edited/deleted messages, attachments, transcripts, oversized or malicious content;
   - channel/thread confusion, unauthorized roles/users, replay and duplicate delivery;
   - immutable source-packet integrity and provenance.
2. **Triage, clarification, and workflow-state transitions**
   - prompt injection in requests, attachments, transcripts, and thread replies;
   - unauthorized, ambiguous, stale, or conflicting approvals;
   - replay, TOCTOU, concurrent replies, restart recovery, and state/Discord-thread divergence.
3. **Role/profile/model routing and worker dispatch**
   - route confusion or fallback to a more privileged profile;
   - toolset and side-effect boundary escalation;
   - worker claims of completion without verifiable artifacts/evidence.
4. **Repository-local artifact generation**
   - path traversal, symlink escapes, repository-marker spoofing, writes outside the target repo;
   - generated Spec Kit artifacts that smuggle executable instructions or alter policy/configuration;
   - preservation of auditability and deterministic resume behavior.
5. **Kanban projection and notifications**
   - projection becoming an accidental source of truth;
   - duplicate/misrouted notifications, untrusted links, and loss/corruption of derived state.
6. **Git/local-git/GitHub handoff**
   - branch/remote/repository confusion, credential exposure, destructive git operations;
   - issue/PR creation or merge/automerge occurring without the correct approval evidence;
   - verification that tests, review results, rollback notes, and approval actors are bound to the exact artifact/commit being handed off.

## Proposed automation approval matrix

Please produce and maintain a stage-by-stage matrix with at least:

| Stage/action | Safe to automate by default? | Required authorization | Required evidence | Reversible? | Fail-closed behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Capture source packet and initialize local workflow state | Yes, when intake binding and repo boundary validate | Intake authorization | Immutable packet hash, actor/message IDs, repository identity | Yes | Block and notify; do not create an unbound workflow |
| Ask clarification questions and persist answers | Yes, but never infer approval from prose | Authorized workflow actor for state transition | Message ID, actor, timestamp, prior state hash | Yes | Keep gate blocked |
| Generate/modify local Spec Kit artifacts | Candidate for automation within a sandboxed repo | Role-specific route; no implicit privilege escalation | Diff, tests, artifact hashes, tool/side-effect log | Usually | Stop before write or revert transaction |
| Run tests/static/adversarial checks | Yes, bounded and reproducible | Execution profile authorization | Commands, versions, results, logs | Yes | Mark evidence incomplete; no handoff |
| Create branch/commit | Approval required initially; possibly policy-automatable later | Release/maintainer approval bound to exact diff | Commit/tree hash, base branch, signer/actor | Yes | No remote mutation |
| Create GitHub issue/PR | Explicit approval required | Maintainer/release-captain authorization | Target repo, branch, diff, test evidence, rollback | Yes | Emit packet only |
| Merge, release, or other irreversible remote action | Never autonomous in v1 | Separate explicit approval, ideally two-person for high-risk changes | Exact commit, checks, reviewers, approval audit trail | No/limited | Refuse and surface required approvers |

## Acceptance criteria

- Add a threat model covering the boundaries above, including attacker goals, trust boundaries, assets, abuse cases, and mitigations.
- Define an explicit approval/evidence schema for every side-effect class: `none`, `local-files`, `local-git`, and `remote-github`.
- Specify which actions are **automated**, **approval-gated**, and **human-only/never autonomous**.
- Define nonces or equivalent replay protection, concurrency/version checks, and stale-approval invalidation for workflow gates.
- Prove that approval is bound to the exact workflow state, artifact/diff/commit, target repository, and side-effect scope—not merely to a Discord message or thread.
- Add adversarial tests for prompt injection, unauthorized actors, edited/replayed messages, symlink/path escapes, route escalation, state races, duplicate delivery, and GitHub target confusion.
- Define the minimum audit record and operator-facing refusal/rollback behavior.
- Keep official Spec Kit execution, Kanban mutation, GitHub issue/PR creation, merge, and release behind explicit reviewed gates until the matrix and tests are accepted.

## Non-goals

- Making Discord or Kanban the source of truth.
- Adding a second workflow state engine.
- Enabling broad autonomous GitHub or release automation as part of this review.

## Suggested deliverables

1. `threat-model.md` or equivalent design section.
2. Approval matrix and state-transition invariants.
3. Adversarial test plan plus focused regression tests.
4. Operator runbook for refusal, recovery, rollback, and approval rotation.
5. A follow-up implementation plan that separates low-risk automation from actions requiring explicit human approval.

This should be treated as a maintainer decision/RFC before expanding the factory beyond the current local, fail-closed steel thread.

### Problem or Use Case

Many users spend hours customizing Hermes with their own branding, welcome page, dashboard, icons, widgets, and domain-specific features. In my case, I added Islamic features such as prayer times, Qur'an shortcuts, and personalized branding because I use them every day.

The problem is that when Hermes is updated, many of these customizations are overwritten. As a result, users have to repeat the same work after almost every update. Eventually, many of us stop customizing Hermes altogether because it's too time-consuming to maintain.

### Proposed Solution

Introduce an upgrade-safe customization system that separates the Hermes core from user-owned customizations.
For example:

A protected branding folder (logos, icons, welcome page).
A themes folder.
Custom dashboard widgets.
A plugin/extension directory that is preserved during upgrades.
A clear distinction between core files and user customization files.

This would allow Hermes to continue receiving frequent updates while ensuring users don't lose their branding, dashboard improvements, or custom features. It would make Hermes a much stronger platform for developers, businesses, educators, and community projects building on top of it.

### Alternatives Considered

Rather than modifying the Hermes core, I believe the platform should provide an official, upgrade-safe customization architecture.

Possible approaches include:

- Protected Branding Directory – A dedicated location for user logos, icons, splash screens, welcome pages, and branding assets that is never overwritten during updates.
- Theme System – Official support for custom themes, colours, fonts, layouts, and UI styling that survives upgrades.
- Dashboard Extension Framework – Allow users to add or remove dashboard cards, widgets, quick actions, and home page content without editing core files.
- Plugin/Extension Directory – A protected location where custom features (such as Prayer Times, Islamic shortcuts, calendars, business tools, education modules, or AI assistants) remain intact after upgrades.
- Custom Configuration Layer – Separate user configuration from the Hermes core so updates replace only the engine while preserving user preferences and customisations.
- Migration/Compatibility Tool – If breaking changes are unavoidable, provide an official migration process that automatically restores compatible user customisations after an update.
- Developer API – Publish stable extension points so developers can integrate with Hermes without patching internal source files that are likely to change.

The long-term goal should be a clear separation between the Hermes runtime and user-owned customisations.

This would allow Hermes to continue shipping frequent updates while giving developers confidence that their branding, dashboard, extensions, and domain-specific improvements will not disappear after every release.

In my opinion, this would make Hermes a much stronger platform for developers, businesses, educators, researchers, and community projects that want to build long-term products on top of Hermes rather than repeatedly modifying the core application.

items.title: **computer_use unusable under WSL: cua-driver manifest's Windows-form `mcp_invocation.command` is passed untranslated to Linux subprocess (and doctor shows a false green)**

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
### Bug Description

On a WSL2 install driving a Windows-side cua-driver, every `computer_use` call fails before the MCP session starts:

```
computer_use backend unavailable: cua-driver session setup failed:
[Errno 2] No such file or directory:
'C:\Users\<user>\.cua-driver\packages\releases\0.7.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\cua-driver.exe'
```

The driver itself is healthy (`cua-driver 0.7.1`, UI Automation reachable, screen capture reachable), and `hermes doctor` / `hermes computer-use doctor` report everything green. The failure is in Hermes: `_resolve_mcp_invocation()` asks the driver for its manifest and returns `mcp_invocation.command` verbatim. A Windows driver reports its own path in native Windows form, which Linux `subprocess` cannot exec, so the stdio MCP spawn dies with ENOENT.

Verified present at v0.18.2 (git install, HEAD b03c94dbe) and byte-identical in `tools/computer_use/cua_backend.py` at current `origin/main` (915f1bf, 2026-07-13).

## Doctor false green

`hermes doctor` / `hermes computer-use doctor` validate the binary and the Windows-side capabilities but never exercise the manifest-to-MCP startup path, so the install reports fully healthy while every real call fails. Suggest doctor additionally resolve the MCP invocation and check the resulting command is spawnable (that one check would have caught this).


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Windows host with cua-driver installed natively (any version recent enough to support the `manifest` subcommand).
2. Hermes running inside WSL2 with the computer_use toolset enabled and the driver command resolving to the `/mnt/c/...` exe.
3. `hermes doctor` / `hermes computer-use doctor`: all green.
4. Call any `computer_use` action (e.g. `list_apps`): ENOENT on the Windows-form path shown above. 100% reproducible.

### Expected Behavior

Hermes agent uses computer_use and starts building stuff while implementing my plans and projects while I work 9.5 to get the fuck out of this rat race...

### Actual Behavior

computer_use is completely unusable on WSL installs as soon as the installed cua-driver is new enough to answer `manifest`, and doctor masks the failure. Happy to send the diff above as a PR with a regression test if wanted.

### Affected Component

Skills (skill loading, skill hub, skill guard), Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
- Hermes Agent v0.18.2 (2026.7.7.2), git install, HEAD b03c94dbe; file confirmed unchanged at origin/main 915f1bf
- Python 3.11.15, WSL2 (Ubuntu, kernel 6.6.114.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2) on Windows 10 (build 19045)
- cua-driver 0.7.1 installed Windows-side via install.ps1; resolved driver command points at the WSL-mounted exe (`/mnt/c/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Programs/Cua/cua-driver/bin/cua-driver.exe`), which spawns fine through WSL interop
```

### Operating System

Windows 10 - WSL2

### Python Version

_No response_

### Hermes Version

_No response_

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`tools/computer_use/cua_backend.py`, `_resolve_mcp_invocation()` (lines ~144-195 at b03c94dbe). The function runs `cua-driver manifest` (the #47072 surface-8 discovery hop, trycua/cua#1961) and returns the manifest's command verbatim:

```python
    command = invocation.get("command")
    ...
    return command, args
```

Under WSL the driver is a Windows binary, so its manifest reports `mcp_invocation.command` as a native Windows path:

```
C:\Users\<user>\.cua-driver\packages\releases\0.7.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\cua-driver.exe
```

That string is handed to the stdio MCP spawn as-is. Linux `subprocess` can exec a Windows exe through WSL interop, but only via its `/mnt/...` form; the drive-letter form is ENOENT. `wslpath -u` translates it to a path that exists:

```
/mnt/c/Users/<user>/.cua-driver/packages/releases/0.7.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/cua-driver.exe
```

Why this regressed silently: every fallback branch in `_resolve_mcp_invocation()` (no `manifest` verb, non-zero exit, junk JSON, missing `command`) keeps the already-resolved `driver_cmd`, which is the working `/mnt/c/...` path. So older drivers without manifest support worked, and the break only appears once the installed driver starts answering `manifest` with its own native path.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

Translate drive-letter commands under WSL before building the spawn, falling back to the resolved `driver_cmd` so the function can never return an unspawnable command. We are running exactly this locally:

```diff
--- a/tools/computer_use/cua_backend.py
+++ b/tools/computer_use/cua_backend.py
@@ -141,6 +141,46 @@
     return env
 
 
+_WINDOWS_DRIVE_PATH_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Za-z]:[\\/]")
+
+
+def _running_under_wsl() -> bool:
+    return hasattr(os, "uname") and "microsoft" in os.uname().release.lower()
+
+
+def _translate_windows_command_for_wsl(command: str, fallback: str) -> str:
+    """Make a manifest-reported Windows path spawnable from WSL.
+
+    A Windows cua-driver manifest reports ``mcp_invocation.command`` in
+    native form (drive letter plus backslashes). Linux ``subprocess``
+    cannot exec that form, so under WSL convert it with ``wslpath -u``.
+    If translation fails or the result does not exist, return ``fallback``
+    (the already-resolved driver command) so we never hand back a command
+    that cannot spawn.
+    """
+    if not _WINDOWS_DRIVE_PATH_RE.match(command):
+        return command
+    if not _running_under_wsl():
+        return command
+    wslpath = shutil.which("wslpath")
+    if not wslpath:
+        return fallback
+    try:
+        proc = subprocess.run(
+            [wslpath, "-u", command],
+            capture_output=True,
+            text=True,
+            timeout=5,
+            stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL,
+        )
+    except Exception:
+        return fallback
+    translated = (proc.stdout or "").strip()
+    if proc.returncode == 0 and translated and os.path.exists(translated):
+        return translated
+    return fallback
+
+
 def _resolve_mcp_invocation(
     driver_cmd: str,
     *,
@@ -192,7 +232,7 @@
         # The driver knows the subcommand but didn't surface its own path.
         # Keep our resolved driver_cmd; the args are still authoritative.
         return driver_cmd, args
-    return command, args
+    return _translate_windows_command_for_wsl(command, driver_cmd), args
 
 # Regex to parse element lines from get_window_state AX tree markdown.
 #
```

No new imports needed (`os`, `re`, `shutil`, `subprocess` are already imported). Non-WSL platforms are unchanged: the helper passes POSIX commands through untouched, and on native Windows Python the WSL gate returns the command as-is.

## Verification on a real install

- Before the patch: every `computer_use` call fails with the ENOENT above.
- After the patch: the full existing `TestMcpInvocationResolution` suite passes (8 tests; they use POSIX-style commands, untouched by the drive-letter gate), and a live `computer_use list_apps` call returns the real Windows app list (15 apps) with the driver spawned Windows-side through interop.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

## Summary

When `busy_input_mode: steer` is enabled, a follow-up can arrive while the model is already generating the final response. At that point `steer()` may no longer be able to inject the text into the active run, so the gateway falls back to the pending queue.

The current normal-completion path then delivers the first response before processing the queued follow-up. The user can therefore receive two fragmented responses even though both messages were sent before any assistant response became visible.

`interrupt` is not a good substitute because it aborts the active run and can leave the original request without a final answer.

## Current behavior and important invariant

The queued fallback appears to be serial, not concurrent: the pending follow-up is processed after the first run completes, using the updated conversation history. This means the second turn should be able to account for the first request and response.

That invariant should be covered explicitly by regression tests, because a race here could otherwise produce two turns that do not share the expected context, duplicate work, or leave the original request unresolved.

## Generic reproduction

1. Configure the gateway with `busy_input_mode: steer`.
2. Send a request that produces a final model response slowly enough to observe.
3. Before any assistant response is visibly delivered, send a short clarification or correction.
4. Make the clarification arrive after the final model call has started, so live steering is no longer accepted.
5. Observe that the gateway sends the first response and then starts a separate follow-up turn.

## Scope relative to #31642

#31642 proposes assimilating follow-ups only before a turn is committed, with commitment defined by the first tool dispatch or first visible output token. That safely covers the early two-turn case.

This issue concerns the later boundary: the turn may already be committed and may have completed tool work, but its final response has not yet been visibly delivered. Cancel-and-restart is therefore unsafe. The missing policy is whether to consolidate without losing committed work, or to guarantee a strictly serial context-aware continuation.

If maintainers prefer one umbrella issue, this can be folded into #31642 as the committed-turn extension.

## Desired behavior

Either of these policies would be preferable, as long as it is deterministic and tested:

### Option A: consolidate before delivery

If the follow-up arrived before the first response was visibly delivered:

- treat the first response as an unpublished draft;
- preserve completed tool work and side-effect state;
- generate one consolidated response that covers both user messages;
- do not persist hidden draft content as if the user had seen it.

### Option B: guaranteed context-aware continuation

Keep the first response, then process the follow-up as a strictly serial continuation:

- guarantee that the second turn receives the first request and completed response in context;
- never start both turns concurrently for the same session;
- never lose the original request or abort completed tool work;
- ensure the second response clearly accounts for, corrects, or supersedes the first when necessary.

A configurable policy could also be reasonable, but silent timing-dependent behavior should be avoided.

## Acceptance criteria

- A late steer fallback never loses either user message.
- Same-session turns do not run concurrently.
- Completed tool work and external side effects are preserved and verified before continuation.
- Tests cover follow-ups arriving during the final model call and during final stream delivery.
- Tests verify both conversation history and visible delivery order.
- Voice and normal text events use the same safe semantics where possible.

## Related issues

- #31642: pre-output assimilation before the turn is committed
- #60543: steer race around the tool-drain / next-call boundary
- #31328: Telegram voice batching can lose an in-flight response
- #63566: hybrid busy routing for queue vs steer
- #30323: ordering of leftover steer and queued follow-ups
- #58446: visibility of steer / queue / interrupt outcomes

items.title: feat(spec-factory): live UI intake and governed GitHub issue queue feeder
items.body:
## Summary

Add a first-class intake surface for the Discord Spec Factory so a user can submit and refine build requests from the live UI, have the request go through the normal Spec Factory intake flow, and optionally operate a governed automation mode that feeds the next eligible GitHub queue issue into the factory on a cron loop.

The goal is to make the current conversational experience available as a durable, observable workflow without creating a second source of truth or bypassing factory gates.

## User experience

### Live UI / conversational intake

From the Spec Factory live UI (and, where supported, the connected Discord intake surface), a user should be able to:

1. Type a request in the same natural-language style used in the current `#spec-factory` conversation.
2. See the request become an intake/workflow item with its source, repository binding, status, and provenance.
3. Continue the conversation for clarification and refinement in the same UI/thread.
4. Submit the finalized request through the existing Spec Factory pipeline.
5. See the created GitHub issue or other handoff artifact, factory run ID, stage, pending approval gate, and links.

The UI must make clear whether a message is conversational intake, a factory-generated status update, a pending clarification, or a side-effect request. It must not treat a normal status message as a new intake request.

### Automated GitHub issue queue mode

Provide an explicitly enabled automation mode that runs from the UI/configuration and periodically:

1. Lists eligible open GitHub issues for a configured repository/label/filter.
2. Selects the next issue deterministically using configured priority/order rules.
3. Verifies that no active or pending factory run already owns the issue.
4. Submits exactly one issue to the Spec Factory with automation provenance and an idempotency key.
5. Shows the feeder's last run, selected issue, result, skip reason, errors, and next scheduled run in the UI.
6. Leaves the issue open until the configured completion/closure policy is independently verified.

The queue feeder must not blindly submit the next issue, retry a failed submission on intuition, or feed factory-generated messages back into intake.

## Requirements

- Reuse the existing Spec Factory intake and run state; do not add a parallel workflow/state engine.
- Support explicit repository binding and fail closed when the target repository is missing, ambiguous, or unauthorized.
- Persist truthful provenance for UI, Discord, GitHub, and automation-originated requests.
- Make idempotency/replay protection visible and durable using the upstream message identity or an automation schedule-slot/issue identity.
- Enforce active-run, delivered-but-open, duplicate, and stale-state guards before automated submission.
- Preserve the existing confirmation/approval gates. Automation may submit intake, but it must never approve a factory gate, merge a PR, or perform an irreversible GitHub action without the configured authorization.
- Provide pause/resume/disable controls and a visible audit trail for automation mode.
- Show failures and blocked reasons verbatim enough for an operator to diagnose them; do not report a run as complete based only on a worker claim.
- Support safe recovery after process restart without double-submitting an issue.
- Keep GitHub queue state and factory state reconciled without making Discord, Kanban, or the UI the canonical source of truth.

## Acceptance criteria

- A user can submit a natural-language request from the live UI and observe the resulting intake record, factory run/status, pending gate, and handoff links.
- Clarification replies remain attached to the correct intake/thread and cannot be mistaken for a new request.
- The UI distinguishes user intake from factory-generated messages and prevents factory output from being resubmitted.
- A configured cron feeder can select one eligible GitHub issue and submit it once with a verifiable automation origin and idempotency key.
- Running the feeder again for the same schedule slot/issue is a no-op with a visible duplicate/ownership reason.
- An active or pending run blocks selection of another issue according to the configured concurrency policy.
- Restarting the feeder does not cause duplicate submissions.
- The UI exposes enablement, schedule, repository/filter configuration, last decision, next run, active run, errors, and pause/disable controls.
- Pending confirmations and other human gates remain visible and actionable in the existing factory thread/UI; the automation mode cannot confirm them.
- Tests cover duplicate delivery, replay, concurrent feeder ticks, issue ownership, stale state, unauthorized repository binding, factory-output feedback loops, and restart recovery.
- The implementation and UI document the approval/evidence boundary and link to the broader approval-matrix work in #63922.

## Non-goals

- Fully autonomous merge, release, or GitHub issue closure.
- Replacing the Spec Factory's canonical state with GitHub, Discord, Kanban, or the UI.
- Adding a second independent approval or workflow engine.
- Automatically dispatching every GitHub issue without eligibility, ownership, idempotency, and authorization checks.

## Related work

- #63922 — RFC: Adversarial review and automation approval matrix for Discord Spec Factory
- #31992 — feat(kanban): sync GitHub issues into Kanban triage without auto-dispatch
- #31392 — RFC: Agent-native task relay with auto-forking subagents + async human approval gates

session to the profile: session persisted in the profile's `state.db`, SOUL
loaded from the profile home, turns logged under the profile's logs.

`9de9c25f`), the SAME invocation runs the DEFAULT profile:

- session row appears in the DEFAULT `state.db` with the stock
  `You are Hermes Agent…` system prompt (profile SOUL.md exists and loads
  fine when tested directly via `load_soul_md`),
- turn_context logs to the default profile's `agent.log`,
- provider resolution differs from the profile's config (our default-scoped
  turns picked the `custom` fallback provider instead of the configured
  `openai-codex`).

Reproduce:

```
hermes -p <secondary-profile> chat        # or chat --cli
# ask "who are you?" → stock identity; session lands in default state.db
```

Two data points that narrow it:

- `hermes -p <profile> prompt-size` scopes CORRECTLY on 0.18.2 (writes the
  profile's log/caches, builds the profile SOUL into the prompt) — so the
  `-p` argv bootstrap in `hermes_cli/main.py` still works; the loss happens
  somewhere in the chat/TUI init path.
- Workaround: bypass the flag with the env var —
  `HERMES_HOME=<profiles-dir>/<name> hermes chat` scopes correctly
  (verified: session lands in the profile `state.db` with the profile SOUL
  as system prompt).

Gateway-side lanes (`/p/<profile>/` dashboard) are unaffected.

items.title: Write-guard error message conflates "outside HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT" with "protected system/credential file" — agent misdiagnoses and retry-loops

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
`agent/file_safety.py: is_write_denied()` returns a bare bool for four very different denial reasons:

1. exact deny-list hit (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `.env`, `/etc/shadow`, …),
2. deny-prefix hit (`~/.ssh/`, `~/.aws/`, `/etc/systemd/`, …),
3. `mcp-tokens` / `pairing` dirs under a Hermes home,
4. path merely **outside** the `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT` allowlist.

Both call sites in `tools/file_operations.py` (`write_file` ~L1387, `patch_file` ~L1570 on current main) then emit the same message for all four:

```
Write denied: '<path>' is a protected system/credential file.
```

For case 4 this is simply false, and it misleads both the model and the operator. Observed on our deployment (v2026.7.7.2 / app 0.18.2, Docker, `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT=/opt/data`): the agent tried to stage a throwaway helper at `/tmp/trilium_report.py`, was told `/tmp/...` "is a protected system/credential file", concluded `/tmp` was a sensitive path, and burned a retry cycle rediscovering by trial that `/opt/data` works. The end-of-turn file-mutation verifier then (correctly) flagged the failed write, which read to the operator like a credential incident — for what was only an allowlist miss.

Suggestion: return/propagate a denial reason and split the message, e.g.

- cases 1–3: `Write denied: '<path>' is a protected system/credential file.`
- case 4: `Write denied: '<path>' is outside the allowed write roots (HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT=/opt/data).`

Naming the allowed root in the error is safe (it is the agent's own working directory, already visible to it) and turns a dead-end error into a self-correcting one — the model's next attempt lands in the right place without a probe loop.

items.title: [Bug]: Desktop: still-RUNNING background subagents vanish from the UI when the user sends a new message

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
### Bug Description

In the desktop app, `delegate_task` subagents run in the background and outlive
the turn that spawned them. While they run, the status stack / spawn-tree panel
shows them fine and the user can click in to follow their live stream. But the
moment the user sends another message in the same session, every subagent row
for the session disappears — including still-`running`/`queued` ones — and never
comes back. There is no longer any way to see what the running subagents are
doing, and their eventual completion summaries never render either.

Distinct from #53187: that issue is about *completed* async-delegation results
not reaching the desktop (stale sidebar, empty /agents panel after completion).
This one is about *live* subagents being wiped mid-flight by the new turn, plus
the mechanism that makes the wipe permanent. The fix proposed in #53187 does not
address this; the fix below does not address #53187's delivery problem.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the Hermes desktop app, start a chat.
2. Ask the agent to `delegate_task` something long-running (runs in background).
3. While the subagent is running and visible in the status stack, send another
   message in the same session.
4. On `message.start` all subagent rows vanish and never reappear.

### Expected Behavior

Still-running/queued background subagents remain visible (and clickable) across
turns; only the *previous* turn's finished rows get flushed from the display.
When a surviving subagent later completes, its summary renders.

### Actual Behavior

All subagent rows for the session are wiped on `message.start`. All subsequent
`subagent.tool` / `subagent.progress` / `subagent.complete` events for the
still-running subagents are silently dropped, so the rows never return and the
completion summaries are never shown.

### Affected Component

Other

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
Not applicable — pure renderer-state bug in the desktop app, root-caused at
source level below (no backend logs involved). Can run `hermes debug share` on
request.
```

### Operating System

macOS 26.5.2

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.18.2 (2026.7.7.2) · upstream ccb045ba · git install Bug still present on upstream `main` @ ccb045ba7 (verified 2026-07-13).

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-message-stream/gateway-event.ts` — the
`message.start` handler unconditionally wipes the session's entire subagent
store on every new turn (line ~265 on current `main`, ccb045ba7):

```ts
} else if (event.type === 'message.start') {
  ...
  flushQueuedDeltas(sessionId)
  clearSessionSubagents(sessionId)        // ← drops running/queued rows too
  setSessionCompacting(sessionId, false)
  compactedTurnRef.current.delete(sessionId)
  nativeSubagentSessionsRef.current.delete(sessionId)
```

`clearSessionSubagents` (`src/store/subagents.ts`) deletes the whole
per-session list, including entries with status `running`/`queued`.

The wipe is permanent because subsequent events for an already-spawned subagent
cannot recreate the row: the subagent event handler upserts with
`createIfMissing` true only for `subagent.spawn_requested` / `subagent.start`
(gateway-event.ts, `SUBAGENT_EVENT_TYPES` branch):

```ts
upsertSubagent(
  sessionId,
  payload as Record<string, unknown>,
  event.type === 'subagent.spawn_requested' || event.type === 'subagent.start',
  event.type
)
```

and `upsertSubagent` (`src/store/subagents.ts`) returns early:

```ts
if (idx < 0 && !createIfMissing) {
  return
}
```

So after the wipe, all further `subagent.tool` / `subagent.progress` /
`subagent.complete` events for the still-running background subagents are
silently dropped.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

The clear exists to flush the *previous* turn's finished rows from the display,
so keep that behavior but preserve live rows: on `message.start`, prune only
terminal-status entries instead of clearing the session.

```ts
// store/subagents.ts
export function pruneFinishedSessionSubagents(sid: string) {
  const map = $subagentsBySession.get()
  const list = map[sid]
  if (!list?.length) return
  const next = list.filter(item => item.status === 'running' || item.status === 'queued')
  if (next.length === list.length) return
  $subagentsBySession.set({ ...map, [sid]: next })
}
```

and in the `message.start` handler:

```ts
- clearSessionSubagents(sessionId)
+ pruneFinishedSessionSubagents(sessionId)
```

The other `clearSessionSubagents` call site (the Stop action in
`use-prompt-actions/index.ts`) should stay a full wipe — `/stop` genuinely
cancels running background subagents, so dropping their rows there is correct.

Regression test (added to `src/store/subagents.test.ts`): seed running + queued
+ completed rows, prune, assert running/queued survive and still accept a
`createIfMissing=false` completion update. Verified the test fails against the
pre-fix behavior (simulated wipe) and passes with the fix.

Carried locally as commit `d38b47083` on my fork's `patched` branch.

items.title: hermes_tools_mcp_server: params_schema never passed to add_tool() — all MCP tools publish an empty **kwargs schema and drop their arguments

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
`_build_server()` in `agent/transports/hermes_tools_mcp_server.py` fetches each tool's authoritative Hermes schema into `params_schema` (line 155) and the comment above `add_tool()` states *"We use add_tool() for full control over the input schema"* — but `params_schema` is never passed to `add_tool()`, and is never read anywhere else in the file (its only occurrence is the assignment). The installed `mcp` SDK's `FastMCP.add_tool()` has no schema parameter at all:

```
FastMCP.add_tool(self, fn, name=None, title=None, description=None,
                 annotations=None, icons=None, meta=None, structured_output=None)
```

So FastMCP falls back to introspecting the handler, `def _dispatch(**kwargs)`, and every exposed tool is published with an empty var-keyword schema:

```json
{"properties": {"kwargs": {"title": "Kwargs"}}, "required": ["kwargs"], "type": "object"}
```

**Impact — the whole `hermes-tools` MCP surface is unusable from any MCP client:**

1. Tools advertise no parameters, so a model cannot tell how to invoke them.
2. Arguments are dropped at validation (`func_metadata` builds the arg model from the same `**kwargs` signature), so the tool runs with empty input.

Concretely, `web_search(query="anthropic claude")` over MCP reaches the Tavily provider as an empty query:

```
INFO plugins.web.tavily.provider: Tavily search: '' (limit=5)
→ {"success": false, "error": "Tavily search failed: Client error '400 Bad Request' ..."}
```

(Tavily's 400 body is `Query is too short. Min query length is 2 characters.` — the key and payload are fine; the query never arrives.)

The in-process tool path is unaffected — only the MCP transport is.

**Fix:** since this SDK's `add_tool()` can't take a JSON schema, give the dispatch closure a real signature derived from the Hermes schema, so FastMCP generates both the published schema *and* the pydantic arg validator correctly:

```python
_JSON_TO_PY = {"string": str, "integer": int, "number": float,
               "boolean": bool, "array": list, "object": dict}

def _signature_from_schema(schema):
    props = (schema or {}).get("properties") or {}
    required = set((schema or {}).get("required") or [])
    params, annots = [], {}
    for pname, pspec in props.items():
        if pname.startswith("_"):
            continue
        py = _JSON_TO_PY.get((pspec or {}).get("type"), Any)
        ann, default = (py, inspect.Parameter.empty) if pname in required \
                       else (Optional[py], None)
        annots[pname] = ann
        params.append(inspect.Parameter(pname, inspect.Parameter.KEYWORD_ONLY,
                                        annotation=ann, default=default))
    return inspect.Signature(params, return_annotation=str), annots
```

then in `_make_handler`, after defining `_dispatch`:

```python
sig, annots = _signature_from_schema(schema)
_dispatch.__signature__ = sig
_dispatch.__annotations__ = {**annots, "return": str}
```

and drop `None`s before dispatch so unset optionals aren't forwarded:

```python
args = {k: v for k, v in kwargs.items() if v is not None}
return handle_function_call(tool_name, args)
```

Verified locally against `main`. Published schema becomes:

```json
{"properties": {"query": {"title": "Query", "type": "string"},
                "limit": {"anyOf": [{"type": "integer"}, {"type": "null"}], "default": null}},
 "required": ["query"], "type": "object"}
```

and the live call returns `{"success": true, "data": {"web": [...]}}`.

Happy to open a PR if the approach looks right.

items.body:
# Bug: TTS voice selection ignores mismatched global vs profile config

## Component
Desktop / TTS configuration merging

## Environment
- OS: Windows 11 Pro
- Hermes: desktop app
- Profile: selene
- Config paths:
  - Global: `C:\Users\Marti\AppData\Local\hermes\config.yaml`
  - Profile: `C:\Users\Marti\AppData\Local\hermes\profiles\selene\config.yaml`

## Problem
When `tts.edge.voice` or `tts.piper.voice` differs between global and profile configs, the active TTS voice does **not** reliably follow either value. The voice appears to fall back to a default/previous value unless both files contain exactly the same voice name.

This makes per-profile voice customization unreliable on the desktop surface.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Set `tts.provider: edge` with `en-GB-RyanNeural` in both global and profile config.
2. Change global config to `en-GB-SoniaNeural`, but leave profile config at `en-GB-RyanNeural`.
3. Restart desktop app.
4. TTS output still uses Ryan, not Sonia.
5. Repeat with other mismatched combinations (`AbbiNeural`, `EmilyNeural`, `en-GB-Abba-medium` etc.) — same fallback behavior occurs.

## Expected Behavior
Hermes should define and document a clear precedence:
- profile config overrides global config, OR
- global config overrides profile config, OR
- both configs are merged deterministically

Mismatched values should not silently revert to a default voice.

## Actual Behavior
TTS voice remains at an old/default voice when global and profile values differ. Only after both files are set to the same voice does the change reliably take effect.

This also causes repeated `NoAudioReceived` failures when the user accidentally sets an invalid/unavailable voice name in one file and the other file still contains the old working value.

## Workaround
Manually keep `tts.edge.voice` and `tts.piper.voice` identical in both:
- `C:\Users\Marti\AppData\Local\hermes\config.yaml`
- `C:\Users\Marti\AppData\Local\hermes\profiles\<profile>\config.yaml`

Then restart the desktop app.

## Additional Notes
- Desktop backend timeouts (`ECONNRESET` / `Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 15000ms`) were observed intermittently during testing, but this issue is separate from the backend timeout bug.
- Local Piper voice downloads via `piper.download_voices` work; invalid voice names return 404.
- `edge-tts` returned `NoAudioReceived` when given invalid voice names such as `en-GB-AbbiNeural` currently absent from Microsoft's voice list.

## Summary

Hermes Studio auto-updates leave the new embedded Python runtime missing pip dependencies, causing silent failures. This is the **second occurrence** of the same class of bug (v9: missing `.py` source file, v10: missing pip package).

## Environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| OS | Windows 10 Pro |
| Hermes Studio | 0.6.29 |
| Embedded runtime | 0.18.2 (auto-upgraded from 0.17.0) |
| hermes-agent CLI | 0.18.0 |
| Affected provider | minimax-cn (transport: anthropic_messages) |
| Unaffected provider | deepseek (transport: openai_chat) |

## Root Cause

Hermes Studio's desktop runtime (`~/.hermes-web-ui/desktop-runtime/hermes/{version}/win-x64/python/`) is an **independent Python environment**, completely isolated from the CLI venv. When Studio performs a major version upgrade, the new runtime directory is created but **pip dependencies are NOT synced**.

This is the second occurrence (v9: missing source file, v10: missing pip package). Both share the same root cause.

## Proposed Fix

1. **Short-term**: Add a dependency integrity check on Studio startup, auto-triggering `pip install` when packages are missing
2. **Long-term**: Add a `pip sync` step to the Studio version upgrade process

## Workaround

```powershell
$RT = "$env:USERPROFILE\.hermes-web-ui\desktop-runtime\hermes\{version}\win-x64\python\python.exe"
& $RT -m pip install anthropic==0.87.0
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.hermes-web-ui\desktop-runtime\hermes\{version}\win-x64\python\Lib\site-packages\anthropic\__pycache__"
# Restart Hermes Studio
```

---

**CVE note**: `pyproject.toml` and `lazy_deps.py` pin `anthropic==0.87.0` due to CVE-2026-34450 and CVE-2026-34452.

items.body:
## Problem

Both `delegate_subagent` and `delegate_task` have a hardcoded 600s (10 min) timeout with no way to override it via the tool call. For tasks like code reviews of large codebases, 10 minutes is often not enough — the subagent gets killed mid-work despite making progress (18 API calls completed in the case that triggered this).

## Current behaviour

- `delegate_subagent`: no `timeout` parameter in the tool schema. Subagent is killed at 600s.
- `delegate_task`: same — no `timeout` parameter, same 600s cap.

## Proposed change

Add an optional `timeout` parameter to both tools (default 600s to preserve current behaviour). Allow values up to at least 3600s (1 hour). This lets the caller set an appropriate limit based on task complexity:

```
delegate_subagent(goal="Review full codebase...", timeout=1800)
delegate_task(goal="Large refactor...", timeout=3600)
```

## Why 600s is too short

- Code reviews of repos with 6000+ line files require multiple read_file calls + reasoning
- Long refactoring tasks with test runs
- Any task that involves running a test suite (the hermes-lcm full suite takes 34 minutes)
- The 600s default forces callers to artificially constrain task scope, defeating the purpose of delegation

## Impact

No breaking change — default stays 600s. Just adds a knob for cases that need more time.

items.title: [Bug]: Desktop + button "Files/Images/Folder" does not open file dialog
items.body:
## Bug Description

In the Desktop Electron app, clicking the `+` button (composer toolbar) → "Files" / "Images" / "Folder" opens the dropdown menu, but selecting any of these items does nothing — no native file dialog appears. This affects both mouse clicks and keyboard (Enter/Space) interaction.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Hermes Desktop (local backend mode)
2. In the composer area, click the `+` button to open the context menu
3. Click "Files" (or "Images", or "Folder")
4. Observe: the dropdown closes but no file dialog appears
5. Repeat with keyboard: Enter/Space on the focused item → same result

## Expected Behavior

Clicking "Files" opens the native OS file dialog, allowing the user to select files and attach them to the composer as `@file:` refs.

## Actual Behavior

Nothing happens. No console errors in the renderer DevTools. The `window.hermesDesktop.selectPaths()` IPC call is never reached — monkey-patching the preload bridge confirms the call is not made.

## Root Cause Analysis

Two independent issues combine to produce this symptom.

### Root Cause A: Radix `DropdownMenuItem.onSelect` does not fire in the Electron renderer

The `ContextMenuItem` component passes callbacks via Radix's `DropdownMenuItem.onSelect`. In the Electron renderer context, Radix's internal `pointerdown` handler takes 200ms+ (`[Violation] 'pointerdown' handler took 207ms`) and swallows the entire event chain — neither native `click` (even capture-phase) nor Radix's `onSelect` ever reaches the callback.

Related: **#53980** confirms the same class of Radix DropdownMenu event-handling issues in this Electron context, with an upstream Radix fix PR open at radix-ui/primitives#3979. That issue targets the model-picker dropdown (different component), but the root cause — `@radix-ui/react-dropdown-menu` swallowing events in Electron renderer — is the same.

### Root Cause B: Composer picker callbacks fail to route correctly

The `pickContextPaths` and `pickImages` callbacks in `useComposerActions` (`apps/desktop/src/app/chat/hooks/use-composer-actions.ts`) had routing issues in the shipped build that caused them to return early with an empty array under certain conditions, even before reaching `selectDesktopPaths`.

Related: **#56572** (merged 2026-07-02, `fix(desktop): restore remote file picker attachments`) was a prior fix in the same code area — the remote-gateway-aware picker routing — confirming this area has had recurring edge cases.

## Fix Applied

Two changes deployed as a narrow asar patch on the local installation (full Vite rebuild was blocked by workspace dependency corruption in npm/pnpm).

### Fix 1: `apps/desktop/src/app/chat/composer/context-menu.tsx`

`ContextMenuItem` now uses native `onClick` + `onKeyDown` as the primary event path, completely bypassing Radix's `onSelect`. The Radix prop is kept as a secondary fallback for future compatibility.

```tsx
<DropdownMenuItem
  disabled={disabled}
  onSelect={onSelect}                                    // fallback
  onClick={handleSelect ? (e) => { e.preventDefault(); handleSelect() } : undefined}
  onKeyDown={handleSelect ? (e) => {
    if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') {
      e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation(); handleSelect()
    }
  } : undefined}
>
```

### Fix 2: `apps/desktop/src/app/desktop-controller.tsx`

Corrected the routing in `onPickFiles` / `onPickFolders` / `onPickImages` callbacks to ensure they consistently reach `pickContextPaths`/`pickImages` regardless of remote/local mode state.

## Verification

After the patch:
- Files → opens `Add files as context` dialog ✅
- Images → opens `Attach images` dialog ✅
- Folder → opens `Add folders as context` dialog ✅
- Mouse click, keyboard Enter, and Space all work ✅

## Environment

- OS: Windows
- Hermes Desktop (Electron), local backend mode
- radix-ui: ^1.4.3

## Labels

`bug`, `comp/desktop`, `P3`

## Related

- #53980 — same-class Radix DropdownMenu event issue in Electron renderer (different component: model pill → composer `+` button, same underlying `@radix-ui/react-dropdown-menu`)
- #56572 — prior fix for remote file picker attachments (same `selectDesktopPaths` / `useComposerActions` code area)
- #52946 — Desktop project folder picker shows local filesystem when connected to remote gateway (related remote-picker code)

---

items.title: [Bug]: MoA preset editor — changing reference provider triggers defaults explosion from half-filled autosave

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
### Bug Description

When editing a Mixture of Agents preset in the Desktop settings (Settings → Model → Mixture of Agents), changing a reference model's provider causes the entire preset to be silently replaced with hardcoded defaults. The user's custom config is destroyed.

Specifically: selecting a different provider in the reference dropdown causes the provider selection to disappear after ~600ms, a second reference entry appears (OpenRouter with the current default model), and the first reference's provider dropdown renders blank.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Hermes Desktop
2. Go to Settings → Model → scroll to Mixture of Agents
3. Click a reference model's provider dropdown (e.g. Reference 1)
4. Select a different provider (e.g. Kilo Gateway)
5. Wait >600ms without selecting a model from the new provider's dropdown
6. Observe: the provider selection reverts, a new reference appears, and the original reference's provider dropdown is blank

### Expected Behavior

The provider change should be reflected in the UI, the model dropdown should populate with the new provider's models, and the user should be able to select a model at their own pace without the config being destroyed.

### Actual Behavior

After ~600ms, the autosave fires with a half-filled slot (provider set, model empty). The backend rejects the empty-model slot and falls back to hardcoded defaults (`openai-codex/gpt-5.5` + `openrouter/deepseek-v4-pro`), replacing the entire preset. See Root Cause Analysis below.

### Debug Report

Intentionally not uploading personal config/logs via `hermes debug share`. Root cause is fully evidenced from source code analysis below and the linked PR.

### Root Cause Analysis

Three interacting bugs in `apps/desktop/src/app/settings/model-settings.tsx` and `hermes_cli/moa_config.py`:

1. **Half-filled slot autosaved** (`model-settings.tsx:359-367`): `updateMoaSlot()` clears the model to `""` when the provider changes. The 600ms debounced `scheduleMoaSave()` sends this incomplete slot to the backend. `_clean_slot()` in `moa_config.py:80` rejects slots with empty model strings. If ALL slots get rejected, `_normalize_preset():120` falls back to `DEFAULT_MOA_REFERENCE_MODELS` (hardcoded `openai-codex/gpt-5.5` + `openrouter/deepseek-v4-pro`).

2. **Provider dropdown missing `withActive()`** (`model-settings.tsx:994,1073`): The reference and aggregator provider Selects filter to authenticated providers only. When the hardcoded defaults inject `openai-codex` (OAuth-required, unauthenticated), Radix `<Select>` renders a blank trigger. The parallel model dropdown at line 1016 correctly uses `withActive()` but the provider dropdowns do not.

3. **No request ordering guard** (`model-settings.tsx:324-334`): `scheduleMoaSave()` has no generation counter — stale save responses can overwrite newer state via `.then(setMoa)`.

Additionally, `DEFAULT_MOA_REFERENCE_MODELS` in `moa_config.py:13-16` hardcodes `openai-codex/gpt-5.5` (OAuth, unauthenticated by default) — practically guaranteeing bug #2 fires on every fresh install or wiped config.

### Proposed Fix

PR #64158 implements three changes in `model-settings.tsx`:

1. `sanitizeMoaRefsForSave()`: filter out reference slots with empty model before any autosave; skip presets that would end up with zero valid references
2. `withActive()` on both MoA provider Selects (reference slots + aggregator), matching the existing pattern on the model Select
3. Generation counter in `scheduleMoaSave()`: skip `setMoa` if a newer save was scheduled while the request was in flight

### Operating System

macOS 26.5.2 (ARM64)

### Hermes Version

main branch, commit c7e09f257 (post-update)

### Affected Component

Other (Desktop settings UI)

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: feat(plugins): streaming LLM output observer hooks — deltas, interim messages, lifecycle

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: area/streaming
labels.description: Streaming responses: gateway delivery, provider wire

items.body:
## Summary

Add observer-only plugin hooks for the streaming LLM output path: per-delta text events, stream lifecycle events, and interim (mid-loop) assistant messages. This is the extension point for streaming TTS pipelines, live dashboards, and telemetry that today can only see the final response.

Part of the plugin-interface expansion tracking issue (community thread, July 2026).

## Motivation (community asks)

- Hyper: "need hooks for every LLM message before sent to the UI, and from the streaming LLM response... to connect TTS pipes, particularly streaming ones", "access to the stream itself would be great", "also interim messages, not just the final response".

## Current state

- `AIAgent` already has an internal `stream_delta_callback` (`run_agent.py` ~L454, fan-out at ~L4630/L4734) wired by the CLI/gateway/TUI — not reachable from plugins.
- `transform_llm_output` (VALID_HOOKS, `hermes_cli/plugins.py`) fires on **final response text only**.
- `post_llm_call` fires once per completed API call — after the stream is done.
- No hook observes interim assistant messages (text produced on non-final tool-loop iterations).

## Proposed interface (additive)

New observer hooks in `VALID_HOOKS`, fired from the same site that fans out to `stream_delta_callback`:

```
on_stream_start(turn_id, iteration, model, provider, surface)
on_stream_delta(turn_id, iteration, delta: str, kind: "text" | "reasoning")
on_stream_end(turn_id, iteration, final_text, finished: bool, error: str | None)
on_interim_message(turn_id, iteration, text)   # assistant text of a non-final loop iteration
```

Semantics to pin down in design:

- **Observer-only in v1.** Deltas are immutable; no transformed streaming (defer — the mutation semantics/perf story is a separate, harder problem).
- **Never-block contract.** Callbacks run sync in the streaming path; core wraps each in try/except (existing `invoke_hook` isolation) and documents a hard "return immediately, queue internally" rule. Consider a small buffered-queue helper for TTS-style consumers so a slow consumer can't stall time-to-first-token.
- `kind: "reasoning"` deltas gated behind a config opt-in (`plugins.stream_reasoning_deltas: false` default) — no silent reasoning exposure.
- Normalized text only — no provider wire events, no raw SSE frames.
- Fires on every surface that streams (CLI, gateway, TUI) — depends on the hook-delivery-parity work.

## Backward compatibility

New hook names only. Existing hooks (`transform_llm_output`, `post_llm_call`) unchanged. Plugins that don't register the new hooks see zero behavior change. Per-hook `has_hook()` guard keeps the streaming hot path at zero overhead when nothing is registered.

## Security considerations

Delta content is a strict subset of what `transform_llm_output`/`post_llm_call` already expose — no new exposure class. Reasoning deltas are the exception and are opt-in.

## Non-goals

- Mutating/transforming the stream (possible v2, separate design).
- Desktop chat GUI rendering hooks (desktop plugin surface is being designed separately and is out of scope).

## Acceptance criteria

- A fixture plugin builds a working streaming consumer (e.g. prints deltas / feeds a TTS queue) on both CLI and gateway.
- A deliberately slow hook callback cannot delay time-to-first-token beyond the documented bound.
- `has_hook()` short-circuit: benchmark shows no measurable streaming overhead with zero registered hooks.
- Tests: fixture-plugin hook firing per surface; error-isolation test (raising callback doesn't kill the stream).

items.body:
## Summary

Make the tool-approval flow pluggable: an **ApprovalTransport** interface so plugins can deliver approval prompts over custom channels (push app, web UI, a different messaging platform), and an optional, heavily-gated **ApprovalPolicy** interface so trusted plugins can pre-decide approvals programmatically. Fail-closed everywhere; hardline commands remain core-owned and non-delegable.

Part of the plugin-interface expansion tracking issue (community thread, July 2026).

## Motivation (community asks)

- Jakob: "I think I also want to be able to hook into the approval process"; "Maybe I want to have the approval of a toolcall on a different channel or with custom code"; "My usecase would be to build a usability layer for hermes for non-technical people. I don't want them to see an approval dialog".

## Current state

- `tools/approval.py` owns the entire flow: CLI interactive prompt, gateway `/approve`//`/deny` (threading.Event queue, ~L1486), and smart mode (auxiliary-LLM decision).
- `pre_approval_request` / `post_approval_response` hooks exist but are **observers only** — the VALID_HOOKS docs explicitly say "Plugins cannot veto or pre-answer an approval" (`hermes_cli/plugins.py` ~L174).
- `pre_tool_call` can block a tool before it reaches approval, but cannot answer an approval or route it to another channel.

## Proposed interface (additive)

Split **presentation/transport** from **authorization policy** — a plugin that hides the dialog is not automatically authorized to approve the action.

### 1. ApprovalTransport (lower trust — presents, human still decides)

```python
class ApprovalTransport(ABC):
    name: str
    def present(self, request: ApprovalRequest) -> ApprovalDecision:
        """Deliver the prompt to a human somewhere; block (with timeout)
        until a decision comes back. Decision ∈ once/session/always/deny/timeout."""
```

- Registered via `ctx.register_approval_transport(transport)`.
- Selected via `security.approval.transport: <name>` in config.yaml. Unset = today's built-in surfaces, unchanged.
- Transport errors/timeouts fall back to the built-in surface, or deny after the existing 5-minute timeout — never silently approve.
- Existing observer hooks keep firing around it (audit continuity).

### 2. ApprovalPolicy (high trust — optional, per-plugin opt-in)

```python
class ApprovalPolicy(ABC):
    def decide(self, request: ApprovalRequest) -> Optional[str]:
        """'approve' | 'deny' | None (pass through to interactive flow)."""
```

- Gated per plugin: `plugins.entries.<id>.allow_approval_policy: true`. Default **off**. Installing/enabling a plugin never grants this — it is a separate, explicit config act (same trust-gate pattern as `allow_tool_override`, #23194).
- **Core-enforced floor:** hardline commands (`detect_hardline_command`) and user deny-rules are checked BEFORE policy consultation and can never be approved by a plugin. Policy can only auto-approve what interactive approval could approve.
- Every policy decision logged (`agent.log` + existing `post_approval_response` observer with `decided_by: "plugin:<id>"`).
- Exceptions in `decide()` = pass-through to interactive (fail closed).

## Backward compatibility

No transport/policy configured → byte-identical behavior. Observer hooks unchanged. Additive config keys only.

## Security considerations (this is the highest-risk item in the batch)

- Threat model: a malicious/compromised plugin with `allow_approval_policy` is equivalent to approval-mode "always allow" — the config gate must say so in its docs.
- Fail-closed on every path: transport error, policy exception, timeout.
- Non-bypassable core floor (hardline detection, user deny rules, sudo stdin guard).
- Zero-mock live tests required on the deny/kill path per repo convention for security-sensitive changes.

## Non-goals

- A generic "suppress all approvals" switch (that's approval mode config, exists today).
- Desktop GUI approval UI (out of scope — separate design track).

## Acceptance criteria

- E2E: approval prompt routed to a custom channel by a fixture transport plugin on a live gateway; decision honored; timeout denies.
- Policy plugin auto-approves an allow-listed pattern; the same plugin CANNOT approve a hardline command (live test, no mocks).
- Enabling the plugin without the config gate leaves policy inactive with a logged warning.
- Docs: threat-model section in the plugins guide.

items.title: feat(plugins): inter-plugin event bus with declared emits/listens contracts
items.body:
## Summary

Give plugins a first-class, namespaced event bus so plugin↔plugin interaction becomes a declared, testable contract instead of ad-hoc imports: `ctx.emit()` + `ctx.subscribe()` with `emits:`/`listens:` declarations in the manifest.

Part of the plugin-interface expansion tracking issue (community thread, July 2026).

## Motivation (community asks)

- blockcipher: "Reactivity would be really frickin' cool. Right now, Hermes Agent plugins advertise capabilities but two plugins interacting with each other is very ad-hoc. Pi lets you specify 'my plugin listens to events emitted by so-and-so's plugin' and the core has an event bus, so there's a testable contract."
- teknium: "In minecraft cross mod compat is probably the biggest issue so it would be good to solve this and allow dependencies on other plugins etc."

## Current state

- `invoke_hook()` is strictly core→plugin. There is no public API for a plugin to emit an event.
- `register_hook()` stores unknown hook names (forward-compat, `hermes_cli/plugins.py` ~L1158) — so two colluding plugins *can* abuse `invoke_hook` for custom names today, but with no namespacing, no declaration, no collision protection, and no discoverability.

## Proposed interface (additive)

```python
# emitter (namespace enforced = the plugin's registry key)
ctx.emit("thing_happened", payload={...})       # delivered as "myplugin:thing_happened"

# listener
ctx.subscribe("otherplugin:thing_happened", callback)
```

- **Namespacing:** plugin events are always `<plugin_key>:<event>`. The bare/core namespace (and a reserved `hermes:` prefix) cannot be emitted by plugins — core lifecycle hooks stay core-owned.
- **Manifest declarations (feeds manifest v2):** `emits: [thing_happened]`, `listens: [otherplugin:thing_happened]`. Declarations are advisory metadata in v1 — used by `hermes plugins show`, the Plugin Doctor (#46456), and pack tooling to surface contracts; undeclared emits log a warning, not an error.
- **Semantics:** fire-and-forget observers with the same per-callback try/except isolation as `invoke_hook`; deterministic delivery order (subscription order); recursion-depth cap (an event handler emitting events that re-trigger it terminates with a logged warning); sync-first, async callbacks handled via the existing loop-safe hook work (PR #63240).
- Return values ignored in v1 (pure pub/sub). Request/response patterns are a non-goal.

## Backward compatibility

Fully additive: new ctx methods, new optional manifest fields. Existing custom-hook-name usage keeps working (grandfathered, with a deprecation-free migration note in docs).

## Security considerations

- Events are in-process, same trust domain as hooks — no new privilege. Payloads should not carry secrets (docs note; same rule as hook payloads).
- Namespace enforcement prevents a plugin from spoofing core lifecycle events into other plugins' handlers.

## Non-goals

- Cross-process / multi-profile messaging (the Agent Message Bus proposal, #42349, is a separate track).
- Guaranteed delivery, persistence, replay.
- RPC / request-response between plugins.

## Related

- #46456 (Plugin Doctor — should validate emits/listens)
- Manifest v2 sub-issue (declaration fields)
- Dependency sub-issue (a `listens:` on another plugin often implies an `optional_plugins` relationship)

## Acceptance criteria

- Two fixture plugins communicate via a declared event, verified in tests.
- Recursion cap test: mutually-emitting plugins terminate cleanly.
- Namespace spoofing test: `ctx.emit` cannot produce a `hermes:`-prefixed or foreign-prefixed event.
- `hermes plugins show <name>` displays emits/listens.

## Summary

Extend `plugin.yaml` with an additive v2 schema: API version, plugin dependencies (with version ranges and load-order resolution), pip dependency declarations, config schema, and richer metadata. All new fields optional — every existing v1 manifest keeps loading unchanged.

Part of the plugin-interface expansion tracking issue (community thread, July 2026).

## Motivation (community asks)

- TunaCookie: "need a base schema i guess, put in author etc" / "need a base schema that everyone follows".
- teknium: "In minecraft cross mod compat is probably the biggest issue so it would be good to solve this and allow dependencies on other plugins etc."
- Prerequisite for plugin packs and the event-bus emits/listens declarations.

## Current state

- `PluginManifest` (`hermes_cli/plugins.py` ~L280): `name`, `version`, `description`, `author`, `requires_env`, `provides_tools`, `provides_hooks`, `kind`, `key`. No schema version, no dependencies, no config schema, no tags.
- Load order is scan order; name collisions resolve by source precedence (bundled < user < project < entrypoint). No inter-plugin ordering control.
- pip dependencies have no first-class seam — #15220 (dependency installation seam), #40287 (`hermes update` removes plugin pip deps), #53272 (memory provider deps not reinstalled).
- Skills already have a config-interface precedent (`metadata.hermes.config` → prompted at setup, stored under `skills.config.<key>`).

## Proposed manifest v2 (all fields optional)

```yaml
name: my-plugin
version: 1.2.0
description: ...
author: ...
license: MIT
homepage: https://github.com/owner/repo
api: 2                      # plugin API schema version; absent = 1
hermes: ">=2.1"             # supported hermes-agent range (advisory warning, not hard fail)
tags: [gateway, telegram]
depends:
  - plugin: other-plugin    # registry key
    version: ">=1.0,<2"     # PEP 440 range
    optional: false
pip_dependencies:
  - "somepkg>=1.0,<2"       # installed via the seam from #15220; survives hermes update
config_schema:              # prompted/validated keys under plugins.entries.<id>.config
  api_url: {type: str, default: "", description: "..."}
emits: [thing_happened]     # event bus declarations (see event-bus sub-issue)
listens: [otherplugin:thing_happened]
```

### Dependency resolution semantics

- Topological load order among enabled plugins; deterministic tie-break (alphabetical by key).
- Cycle detection → all plugins in the cycle fail to load with a clear diagnostic naming the cycle.
- Missing required dep → dependent plugin does not load; `hermes plugins list` shows why; `hermes plugins enable X` suggests enabling the dep.
- Missing optional dep → loads normally; `ctx.has_plugin("name")` for runtime probing.
- **No auto-download of plugin code.** Enabling a plugin never fetches other plugins. `hermes plugins install` MAY prompt to install declared deps (explicit consent, like pack install).
- Version-range violation → warning + load (advisory in v1 of this feature; strictness can be a config knob later).

### pip_dependencies seam

Consolidates #15220/#40287/#53272: declared pip deps are recorded, installed at `hermes plugins install`/`enable` time (with the usual supply-chain pinning rules — upper bounds required), and re-applied by `hermes update`.

## Backward compatibility

- `api` absent → treated as v1; parser defaults preserve today's behavior for every existing manifest.
- Unknown fields already ignored by `_parse_manifest` — v2 manifests degrade gracefully on older Hermes (fields ignored), modulo the `hermes:` range warning they can't see.
- No changes to `register(ctx)` contract.

## Security considerations

- pip installs follow the dependency-pinning policy (upper bounds mandatory).
- No transitive plugin auto-install — dependency resolution orders and gates, it never fetches.

## Non-goals

- A hosted registry/marketplace (separate ecosystem track).
- Hard version pinning between plugins (advisory ranges first).

## Acceptance criteria

- v1 fixture manifests from the existing test suite load byte-identically.
- Cycle, missing-dep, and optional-dep fixtures produce the documented diagnostics.
- `hermes update` preserves declared pip deps (regression test for #40287).
- Plugin Doctor (#46456) validates v2 fields.

items.body:
## Summary

Add **plugin packs**: a declarative, shareable file that pins a set of plugins (sources + versions + non-secret config), with `hermes plugins pack export` / `hermes plugins pack install`. Packs are environment definitions — like sharing a modpack — not a new executable plugin type.

Part of the plugin-interface expansion tracking issue (community thread, July 2026).

## Motivation (community asks)

- Hyper: "need plugin packs that can be easily defined and shared... if you have a ton of plugins its gonna be hard to share your setup like you can share an agent profile. so need a way to create a plugin-pack definition and share mechanism" / "or people are gonna waste tons of time trying to configure tons of plugins they saw in some yt vid".
- yairtech: "a collection of Plugins - like Steam does it?"
- teknium: "this is like minecraft modpacks haha".

## Current state

- `hermes plugins install owner/repo` installs one plugin from GitHub (`hermes_cli/plugins_cmd.py`).
- `plugins.enabled` / `plugins.disabled` / `plugins.entries.<id>` in config.yaml hold activation + per-plugin settings.
- Profiles (`hermes -p`) share a whole instance; there is no portable artifact for "this set of plugins, configured like this".

## Proposed interface

`pack.yaml` (shareable single file):

```yaml
pack:
  name: voice-assistant-pack
  version: 1.0.0
  author: hyper
  description: STT + streaming TTS + approval relay
plugins:
  - source: github:owner/tts-stream-plugin
    version: v1.2.0            # tag/commit pin
    config:                     # non-secret plugins.entries.<id> keys only
      voice: nova
  - source: github:owner/approval-relay
    version: 8f3c2d1
requires_env:                   # secrets prompted at install, never embedded
  - ELEVENLABS_API_KEY
```

CLI:

- `hermes plugins pack export <file>` — snapshot currently enabled user plugins (source, pinned version, sanitized config).
- `hermes plugins pack install <file|url|owner/repo>` — show a full review screen (every plugin, source, version, requested env keys), install on confirm, prompt for `requires_env` via the existing env-var prompt machinery.
- `hermes plugins pack diff <file>` — compare against current state.

Semantics:

- Installing a pack = N ordinary plugin installs + config writes. Nothing new at runtime.
- Version pins are commit/tag-level (supply-chain: no floating `main` by default; warn if a pack uses one).
- **Secrets never serialize into packs.** Export strips anything secret-shaped; `requires_env` is the declared prompt list.
- Pack install respects `plugins.enabled` opt-in flow — plugins arrive enabled only because the user confirmed the review screen.

## Backward compatibility

Purely additive CLI + file format. No changes to plugin loading, manifests parse as before.

## Security considerations

- The review screen is mandatory (no `--yes` in v1) — a pack is arbitrary third-party code times N.
- Version pinning to immutable refs by default.
- Config injection limited to `plugins.entries.<id>.*` namespaces — a pack cannot write arbitrary config.yaml keys (no flipping `security.*`).

## Dependencies

- Manifest v2 + dependency declarations (packs rely on pinnable versions and dep diagnostics).

## Non-goals

- Hosted pack registry/discovery UI (ecosystem track).
- Desktop GUI pack browser (out of scope — separate design).

## Acceptance criteria

- Round-trip: export on machine A → install on clean HERMES_HOME → identical `plugins.enabled` + entries config, secrets prompted.
- Pack attempting to set a non-`plugins.entries` config key is rejected with a clear error.
- E2E test with a two-plugin pack from fixture repos.

items.title: feat(plugins): cache-safe context injection — system prompt sections + environment hints

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Summary

Land cache-safe context injection for plugins: `ctx.register_system_prompt_section()` (evaluated once at session start, stable for the session lifetime) and an environment-hints extension point. This finalizes the design already proposed in #50203 / RFC #58547, with PR #51589 as the candidate reference implementation.

Part of the plugin-interface expansion tracking issue (community thread, July 2026).

## Motivation (community asks)

- ZaynJarvis: "definitely consider context hook as in PI agent".
- Existing asks: #50203 (static_context hook), RFC #58547 (system prompt sections + environment hints), PR #51589 (implementation).

## Current state

- `pre_llm_call` hooks can inject per-turn context — but ONLY into the user message (never system prompt), ephemeral, never persisted (`PluginManager.invoke_hook` docstring, `hermes_cli/plugins.py` ~L1900). This is deliberate: the system prompt must stay byte-stable for the life of a conversation (prompt-caching invariant, AGENTS.md).
- Plugins that need *stable* context (a kanban worker's board rules, a persona layer, an environment descriptor) must re-inject it every turn — wasted tokens — or ship a skill the user must load manually.

## Proposed interface (additive)

```python
def register(ctx):
    ctx.register_system_prompt_section(
        id="myplugin.rules",
        content=lambda session_info: "...",   # str or callable; evaluated ONCE at session start
        position="after_memory",              # coarse anchor, not arbitrary ordering
        max_chars=4000,                        # enforced budget
    )
```

- Evaluated exactly once when the system prompt is assembled for a new session; the result is frozen for the session. Callables that raise → section skipped with a logged warning (never a broken prompt).
- Cache analysis: content is fixed at session start ⇒ the prompt prefix stays byte-stable across every turn of the conversation ⇒ the caching invariant holds. Changing plugin state mid-session does NOT re-render the section (documented; next session picks it up).
- Per-section and total character budgets so plugins can't blow up every conversation's token cost invisibly. Sections logged at session start (`agent.log`) for accountability.
- Environment-hints hook (`build_environment_hints`) appends key-value rows to the existing execution-environment block, same evaluate-once rule.

## Backward compatibility

- New ctx method only. `pre_llm_call` per-turn injection unchanged and remains the right tool for dynamic/recalled context.
- Sections append at defined anchors — existing system prompt content and ordering untouched when no plugin registers a section.

## Security considerations

- System-prompt injection is high-trust by nature — a plugin can already achieve equivalent influence via `pre_llm_call`, so this is not a new privilege class, but sections are visible (`agent.log` + a `hermes plugins show` listing) to keep it auditable.
- Budget caps prevent quiet cost inflation.

## Relationship to existing work

#50203 and #58547 describe this design; PR #51589 (@westkite1201) implements the static hook. Plan: review/salvage #51589 against this spec with contributor credit, extend with budgets + env hints if absent.

## Non-goals

- Mid-session re-rendering of sections (breaks the caching invariant — will not implement).
- Arbitrary reordering/replacement of core system prompt content.

## Acceptance criteria

- Fixture plugin registers a section; system prompt is byte-identical across turns of one session (cache-safety test).
- Section changes take effect on next session only.
- Budget-exceeded and raising-callable cases degrade gracefully with warnings.
